newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq cuts food rations under oil deal with U.N.
newsitem.headline: Iraq cuts food rations under oil deal with U.N.

text.p: Iraq announced on Sunday it was cutting food rations to its people, saying it had not received sufficient supplies under its oil deal with the United Nations because of the United States and Turkey.

Wheat flour and sugar rations will be kept unchanged but other essentials such as rice and pulses sold to Iraqis at giveaway prices will be below the amount the government had earlier promised under the oil deal.
According to the Iraqi News Agency INA each Iraqi will get two kg ( 4.4 lb) of rice in July instead of 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) and half a kg (1.1 lb) of pulses instead of one kg (2.2 lb).

"The reason to hand out two kilograms of rice instead of 2.5 kilograms is because the American administration has blocked rice contracts for three months," INA said, quoting an official source at the trade ministry.

Iraq has been under stringent U.N. sanctions since its troops invaded Kuwait in 1990. But under its deal with the United Nations, Iraq was allowed from December to June to export $2 billion worth of oil to raise money for urgent needs.
The deal was renewed by the U.N. Security Council for another six months from June 8 but Baghdad cannot start oil exports until it hives a food and medicine distribution plan to the United Nations.
Iraq's Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said last week in Vienna where he attended an OPEC meeting that Iraq would start oil exports under the deal in seven to 10 days.

Iraqi and U.N. officials had announced that each Iraq would be entitled to nine kg of flour, 2.5 kg of rice and two kg of sugar. Baby formula, tea and soap rations also rose from levels before the oil programme.

The source said the trade ministry reported the Turkish attack on Kurdish rebels in northern Iraq had "led to blocking the arrival of foodstuffs including pulses." Turkish forces, after a six-week campaign against Kurdish rebels, have now mostly withdrawn.
While oil exports had gone smoothly in the first six months of the deal, INA said only 38 per cent of food that Baghdad had ordered from foreign firms under the pact had reached Iraq.
It said Iraq had received only 61 tonnes of medicine and about 850,000 tonnes of food out of more than two million tonnes Iraq ordered.
Iraq has repeatedly blamed Washington, which led the coalition that drove it from Kuwait in 1991, for delays in food and medicine deliveries. Washington, in turn, has often blamed delays on Baghdad.
